function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
When you’re dealing with “currency valuations over time” you’re essentially looking at a **time‑series** problem. Below are some common ways to model this data, along with their trade‑offs so you can pick what fits your use case best. | Approach | Typical Structure | Pros | Cons | |----------|-------------------|------|------| | **Relational Table** (SQL) | `CREATE TABLE rates (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, base VARCHAR(3), target VARCHAR(3), rate NUMERIC, ts TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE);` | • Mature ecosystem (PostgreSQL, MySQL).
• ACID guarantees, joins, indexes.
• Good for ad‑hoc queries, reporting. | • Scaling to millions of rows per second can be costly.
• Requires schema migrations for new columns. | | **Time‑Series DB** (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, VictoriaMetrics) | `INSERT INTO rates(base='USD', target='EUR', rate=0.85, ts='2024‑06‑10T12:00:00Z');` | • Optimized for high write throughput and down‑sampling.
• Built‑in retention policies, continuous aggregates.
• Native support for time‑based queries (`SELECT MEAN(rate) FROM rates WHERE time > now() - 1h`). | • Less flexible for complex joins across unrelated tables.
• Requires learning a new query language (InfluxQL / Flux). | | **Columnar Store** (ClickHouse, Druid) | `INSERT INTO rates VALUES ('USD','EUR',0.85,'2024-06-10 12:00:00');` | • Extremely fast analytical queries over huge datasets.
• Compression and vectorized execution. | • Not ideal for real‑time ingestion unless configured properly.
• Schema changes can be expensive. | | **In‑Memory Pandas DataFrame** (Python) | `df = pd.DataFrame(columns=['base','target','rate','ts']); df.loc[len(df)] = ['USD','EUR',0.85,'2024‑06‑10 12:00:00']` | • Great for prototyping, exploratory analysis.
• Rich ecosystem (NumPy, matplotlib, statsmodels). | • Limited to RAM; not suitable for terabytes of data.
• Persistence requires writing to disk (CSV, Parquet). | | **Key‑Value Store** (Redis, RocksDB) | `SET "USD_EUR:20240610T120000" 0.85` | • Very low latency reads/writes.
• Can store as sorted set (`ZADD rates 1686355200 0.85`) for range queries. | • Lacks built‑in aggregation functions.
• You need to implement logic for down‑sampling, retention. | | **Flat File (CSV/Parquet)** | `rates.csv`: `timestamp,base,target,rate\n2024-06-10T12:00:00Z,USD,EUR,0.85` | • Simple, portable, easy to version control.
• Parquet offers columnar compression. | • Not great for incremental writes without rewriting entire file.
• Query performance depends on tooling (Pandas, Spark). | ### Choosing the Right One | Scenario | Recommended Choice | Why | |----------|--------------------|-----| | **Real‑time ingestion + long‑term analytics** | **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL + hypertables) | Combines SQL familiarity with time‑series optimizations. | | **High‑frequency tick data (millions of updates per second)** | **InfluxDB** or **ClickHouse** | Designed for massive write loads and efficient roll‑ups. | | **Ad‑hoc exploration in a notebook** | **Pandas DataFrame** | Fast prototyping, interactive visualisation. | | **Low‑latency look‑ups for a single currency pair** | **Redis Sorted Set** | O(log N) range queries, in‑memory speed. | | **Data sharing / archival** | **Parquet files on S3** | Columnar storage, compression, works with Athena/Spark. | ### Practical Tips 1. **Index on `(base, target, ts)`** – ensures fast look‑ups for a specific pair over a time window. 2. **Use UTC timestamps** – avoids daylight‑saving headaches. 3. **Store as numeric types** – avoid string parsing during queries. 4. **Down‑sample older data** – keep raw data for the last week/month, then aggregate to hourly/daily for older periods. 5. **Version your schema** – add a `version` column or use a separate table for metadata if you anticipate adding new fields (e.g., bid/ask spreads). --- #### Quick Example: TimescaleDB Hypertable ```sql -- Create base table CREATE TABLE rates ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, base CHAR(3), target CHAR(3), rate DOUBLE PRECISION, ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL ); -- Convert to hypertable SELECT create_hypertable('rates', 'ts'); -- Insert INSERT INTO rates (base, target, rate, ts) VALUES ('USD', 'EUR', 0.85123, '2024-06-10T12:00:00Z'); -- Query last hour’s average SELECT avg(rate) FROM rates WHERE base='USD' AND target='EUR' AND ts >= now() - INTERVAL '1 hour'; ``` This gives you SQL semantics plus automatic partitioning and compression. --- ### Bottom Line If you’re building a production system that needs to ingest thousands of updates per second and run heavy analytics, go with a dedicated time‑series database (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, ClickHouse). For quick experiments or small‑scale projects, a Pandas DataFrame or a simple CSV/Parquet file will do. And if you only need ultra‑fast look‑ups for a handful of pairs, Redis sorted sets can be a lightweight solution.
